title: Index arithmetic (interval length, midpoint, slice, wrap)
description: The +1 / -1 / midpoint / modulo idioms behind sliding windows, binary search, fixed-length slices, and circular indexing — the arithmetic you reach for before the algorithm.

conversation.intro: How you'd talk through index arithmetic in an interview when it's the load-bearing detail (off-by-one bugs, sliding-window bounds, midpoint overflow). Each section: what you'd say, then why that move matters.

sections.title: 1. Why drill this?
sections.prompt: Index math is the silent killer of interview problems.
sections.say:
"Index arithmetic is what trips me up under time pressure — `r - l` vs `r - l + 1`, slice's exclusive end vs inclusive, midpoint formulas, negative-index wrapping. None of it is hard, but ALL of it is load-bearing: a one-off on the window length and the sliding-window solution silently returns the wrong answer for half the inputs. I want the five formulas in my hands so I spend interview time on the algorithm, not the arithmetic."

"The five idioms I'd memorize: inclusive length `r - l + 1`, midpoint `(lo + hi) >> 1`, fixed-length slice `arr.slice(start, start + n)`, circular index `((i % n) + n) % n`, nth-from-end `arr[arr.length - n]` (or `arr.at(-n)`)."
sections.why: Most interview bugs aren't conceptual — they're off-by-one. Frame this lesson as a memorized toolkit, not 'derive it on the spot', and you avoid the classic disaster: candidate has the right algorithm shape but the window length is `r - l` instead of `r - l + 1`, every test fails, panic ensues. Saying 'I always reach for `r - l + 1` for inclusive length' moves a class of bugs from 'might happen' to 'won't happen'.

sections.title: 2. The common mistakes first
sections.prompt: What's the actual bug each formula prevents?
sections.say:
"Three bugs I want to head off:"

• "`r - l` for window length. Subtraction undercounts: `arr[2..6]` has 5 elements (indices 2,3,4,5,6), but `6 - 2 = 4`. The +1 IS the left endpoint. Drop it and your sliding-window sums are systematically too small."

• "`Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2)` for midpoint — correct but verbose, and on very large arrays the sum can overflow in languages with fixed ints. JS won't overflow at typical interview sizes, but `(lo + hi) >> 1` reads as 'the idiom' and avoids the issue. The bit-shift right by 1 is integer floor-divide by 2 for non-negative integers."

• "`arr.slice(start, start + n - 1)` thinking the second arg is inclusive. It's NOT. slice's end is EXCLUSIVE — `arr.slice(2, 5)` yields indices 2, 3, 4 (three items). For exactly n items from start, the second arg is `start + n`."

• "`arr[i % n]` for circular access where `i` could be negative. JS `%` keeps the sign of the dividend: `-1 % 4 === -1`, not 3. So `arr[-1]` is undefined, not the last element. The fix is the double modulo: `((i % n) + n) % n` always lands in `[0, n)`."
sections.why: These bugs are all silent — the code runs, just returns wrong answers. Pointing them out unprompted shows the interviewer you've shipped this code, hit these bugs, and remember the fixes. The `%` sign-preservation point in particular is one most candidates don't know — JS borrowed it from C, and it bites every time someone implements a ring buffer naively.

sections.title: 3. Spot the math
sections.say:
"All five formulas come from one principle: arrays are 0-indexed half-open intervals, but humans think in closed intervals. The +1, -1, and modulo dances are all translations between 'count of items' (closed) and 'index positions' (0-indexed)."

• "Inclusive length `r - l + 1`: closing the interval. There are `r - l` GAPS between l and r, plus 1 to count the left endpoint."

• "Midpoint `(lo + hi) >> 1`: arithmetic mean, floor toward 0. The `>> 1` only works because `lo + hi` is non-negative — for general integers you'd want `Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2)`."

• "Fixed-length slice `slice(start, start + n)`: slice takes a half-open interval `[start, end)`, so `end - start` IS the count."

• "Sliding window of size k: when r advances and the window is full, l = r - k + 1, and the element leaving the window on the next slide is `arr[r - k]` (the one just before the new left edge)."

• "Circular `((i % n) + n) % n`: first `%` folds magnitude into `[-(n-1), n-1]`; `+n` shifts to `[1, 2n-1]`; second `%` folds to `[0, n)`. The double-modulo is the cheapest way to guarantee a valid index."
sections.why: Naming the underlying principle — 'half-open intervals + 0-indexed positions' — is what shows you understand the FAMILY of bugs, not just one formula. If the interviewer pivots to a related problem (say, a different language with 1-indexed arrays, or a half-open vs closed range), you can re-derive on the spot instead of being stuck.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a sliding window using the inclusive-length invariant.
sections.intro: "Let me trace `maxWindowSum([2,1,5,1,3,2], 3)` — the L3 case. The invariant: window covers `[r-k+1, r]` inclusive, length k. Element leaving on slide is `arr[r-k]`."

examples.note: Three slides after the seed; max is at the second slide (window [5,1,3]).
examples.trace:
SEED:  i=0..2  sum = 2+1+5 = 8  best=8
SLIDE: r=3  sum += arr[3]-arr[0] = 1-2 = -1  sum=7  best=8
SLIDE: r=4  sum += arr[4]-arr[1] = 3-1 = +2  sum=9  best=9  ★
SLIDE: r=5  sum += arr[5]-arr[2] = 2-5 = -3  sum=6  best=9
return 9  ✓

examples.note: Negative-index wrap — JS `arr[-1]` is undefined, but the double-modulo dance lands on the last element.
examples.trace:
n=4, i=-1
step 1: -1 % 4 = -1     (JS keeps sign of dividend)
step 2: -1 + 4 = 3
step 3: 3 % 4 = 3
arr[3] = 'd'  ✓

sections.why: The sliding-window trace is the load-bearing one — it surfaces the `arr[r-k]` formula for the element leaving the window. Most candidates either re-derive that bound mid-solution or guess wrong; tracing once on numbers makes it stick. The circular-index trace is the one to keep ready for any 'ring buffer / round robin' follow-up — the formula looks arcane until you see the three steps.

sections.title: 5. Edges + pitfalls
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up the formulas?
sections.say:
"Edges to flag:"

• "Empty array — `arr.slice(0, 0)` and `arr.slice(0, n)` for `n=0` are both empty, which is the right answer. Inclusive length on `l=0, r=-1` would give 0, also right. The formulas degrade gracefully."

• "Single-element array — `r - l + 1` with `l = r` gives 1. `arr.slice(0, 1)` gives one item. Midpoint of `lo=0, hi=0` is 0. All sane."

• "Negative slice second arg — `arr.slice(0, -1)` drops the LAST element (slice treats negative end as `length + end`). Useful for 'all but last', but a common confusion: it does NOT throw, it silently returns a shorter array."

• "`arr.at(-1)` vs `arr[arr.length - 1]` — both work, but `at` is the modern idiom and handles negative indices natively. `arr[-1]` is the trap that returns undefined."

• "Midpoint overflow — at typical interview sizes JS numbers handle `lo + hi` fine (Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER is ~9 quadrillion). The defensive idiom `lo + ((hi - lo) >> 1)` is worth knowing but overkill in JS interviews."
sections.why: The negative-slice-end behavior is the one to mention if asked to write a 'drop the last element' helper — most candidates write `arr.slice(0, arr.length - 1)` and miss that `arr.slice(0, -1)` is shorter and idiomatic. Showing that you know JS's slice semantics on negative ends signals you've actually read the MDN docs at least once.

sections.title: 6. Complexity
sections.prompt: How would you justify the operation costs?
sections.say:
"Each formula is O(1) on its own — pure arithmetic. The complexity shows up in how they're USED:"

• "Sliding window with the `arr[r] - arr[r-k]` slide: O(n) total. You touch each element exactly twice (once on entry, once on exit), so the sum across all slides is 2n = O(n). Without the slide formula you'd recompute the window sum every step, which would be O(n·k)."

• "Midpoint `(lo + hi) >> 1` enables O(log n) binary search by halving the range each step. The bit-shift itself is O(1); the halving structure is what gives the log."

• "Circular indexing is O(1) read/write on a fixed-size ring buffer — that's the whole reason ring buffers exist, vs growing an array and paying O(n) on shift."

• "`slice` returns a NEW array — O(k) time and space for k items. If you only need to ITERATE the slice, a `for` loop with `start..start+n` indices is O(k) time but O(1) extra space."

"If you want me to extend: the sliding-window slide formula is the building block for the longest-substring-without-repeats and minimum-window-substring patterns — both use the same `arr[r] - arr[r-k]` arithmetic but with a hash-counter playing the role of the running sum."
sections.why: Tying each formula to the O(...) cost of the pattern that USES it is what turns 'memorized arithmetic' into 'understood tool'. The slice-allocation point in particular is the kind of constant-factor awareness that distinguishes a 3-year engineer from a 1-year one: anyone can write `arr.slice(...)`, but knowing it allocates is what stops you from using it inside a tight loop.

walkthrough.intro: Step through `maxWindowSum([2,1,5,1,3,2], 3)` — the L3 canonical. The window-length invariant is `k = r - l + 1`, and on each slide the element leaving is `arr[r - k]`. Two examples vary k and the input to show the invariant holds.
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter — arr=${JSON.stringify(arr)}, k=${k}`, state: { arr, k } };
yield { line: 2, label: `init sum = 0`, state: { arr, k, sum } };
yield { line: 3, label: `seed: sum += arr[${i}]=${arr[i]} → sum=${sum}`, state: { arr, k, sum, i, window: arr.slice(0, i + 1) } };
yield { line: 4, label: `best = sum = ${best} (seed window covers indices 0..${k - 1}, length ${k} = r-l+1)`, state: { arr, k, sum, best, window: arr.slice(0, k) } };
for (let r = k; r < arr.length; r++) {

yield { line: 7, label: `slide r=${r}: entering arr[${r}]=${entering}, leaving arr[${r - k}]=${leaving} (window now [${r - k + 1}..${r}])`, state: { arr, k, sum, best, r, entering, leaving, window: arr.slice(r - k + 1, r + 1) } };
yield { line: 8, label: `sum += ${entering} - ${leaving} = ${entering - leaving} → sum=${sum}`, state: { arr, k, sum, best, r, window: arr.slice(r - k + 1, r + 1) } };
yield { line: 9, label: `sum=${sum} > prev best → best=${best} ★`, state: { arr, k, sum, best, r, window: arr.slice(r - k + 1, r + 1) } };
yield { line: 9, label: `sum=${sum} ≤ best=${best} → keep best`, state: { arr, k, sum, best, r, window: arr.slice(r - k + 1, r + 1) } };
yield { line: 11, label: `return best = ${best}`, state: { arr, k, sum, best, returns: best } };

reference.approach: Fixed-size sliding window — seed k, then slide with arr[r] - arr[r-k]
notes: Inclusive length needs +1 because subtraction undercounts the left endpoint.
`(lo + hi) >> 1` is the idiomatic floor-divide for midpoint — interviewers expect it over `Math.floor((lo+hi)/2)`.
`slice(start, start + n)` gives exactly n items because slice's end is EXCLUSIVE — a frequent off-by-one source.
JS `%` keeps the sign of the dividend, so wrapping a negative index needs `((i % n) + n) % n`, not just `i % n`.

questions.q: How many elements are between indices l=2 and r=6, INCLUSIVE of both endpoints?
questions.explain: Inclusive length is r - l + 1. The +1 counts the left endpoint that the subtraction would otherwise drop.

questions.q: Binary search: what is the midpoint of lo=3 and hi=10 using `(lo + hi) >> 1`?
questions.explain: (3 + 10) >> 1 = 13 >> 1 = 6. Right-shift by 1 is integer divide by 2 (floor).

questions.q: You want a sub-array of exactly 4 elements starting at index 2. Which call?
questions.explain: slice's 2nd arg is EXCLUSIVE, so end = start + n gives exactly n items. arr.slice(2, 4) returns only 2 elements.

questions.q: What does `arr[-1]` return in JavaScript when arr = [10, 20, 30]?
options: undefined — JS arrays don't support negative bracket indices
questions.explain: JS array bracket access with a negative index is just a missing property lookup → undefined. Use `arr.at(-1)` for the Python-style behavior.

L3.prompt: Write `maxWindowSum(arr, k)` that returns the maximum sum over any sliding window of size k, using r - l + 1 = k as the window-length invariant. Log `maxWindowSum([2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], 3)`.
hints: Seed `sum` with the first k elements, then slide.
When the right pointer advances to r, the element leaving the window is arr[r - k] (because window length k = r - l + 1 means l = r - k + 1).
